article_title: ChatGPT improves creative problem-solving performance in university students: An experimental study
citation: Urban, M., Děchtěrenko, F., Lukavský, J., Hrabalová, V., Svacha, F., Brom, C., & Urban, K. (2024). ChatGPT Improves Creative Problem-Solving Performance in University Students: An Experimental Study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105031
title: Hybrid human-AI regulation (HHAIR) theory as applied to metacognitive demands of ChatGPT-assisted problem-solving
description: Hybrid human-AI regulation theory (attributed to Molenaar) holds that working with generative AI demands strong metacognitive skills because learners combine their own ideas with AI output: they must "select relevant information, reiterating and clarifying ideas, debugging errors, and adjusting their approach to ensure coherence and meaningfulness." The study uses the theory to motivate hypotheses about self-efficacy, monitoring accuracy, metacognitive experiences, and mental effort when solving ill-defined tasks with ChatGPT, and concludes that effective regulation requires students to attend to valid metacognitive cues rather than perceived ease.
requirements: Learners must possess or develop metacognitive monitoring and self-evaluation skills to assess AI-generated and self-generated ideas
Students must perform accurate self-evaluation of final outcomes containing both student- and ChatGPT-generated ideas
constraints: The study reports that perceived ease and usefulness act as invalid cues, so regulation based on metacognitive experiences alone may be inaccurate
target_learners: university students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and self-evaluation of AI-assisted work
examples: The preregistered experiment measured self-efficacy, self-evaluation bias, task interest, difficulty, and mental effort with and without ChatGPT during a Product Improvement Task
key_sources: Urban, M., Děchtěrenko, F., Lukavský, J., Hrabalová, V., Svacha, F., Brom, C., & Urban, K. (2024). ChatGPT Improves Creative Problem-Solving Performance in University Students: An Experimental Study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105031

article_title: Scenario-based simulation training for the WHO hand hygiene self-assessment framework.
citation: Tartari E, Fankhauser C, Peters A, Sithole BL, Timurkaynak F, Masson-Roy S, Allegranzi B, Pires D, Pittet D. (2019). Scenario-based simulation training for the WHO hand hygiene self-assessment framework. Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13756-019-0511-9
title: Three case scenario-based simulations for HHSAF completion training
description: WHO and the WHO Collaborating Centre developed an educational video, a promotional video and "three case scenario-based simulations (Tables 1, 2 and 3) for IPC specialists to simulate and fully assimilate the correct completion of the HHSAF framework in a standardized format". The scenarios depict a tertiary care centre (scored Advanced, 377.5/500), a rural Ugandan teaching hospital (Inadequate, 80/500) and a national referral hospital (Basic, 120/500), spanning a range of contexts and resource levels including low-resource settings.
requirements: Use by professionals in charge of implementing a hand hygiene improvement strategy
Use prior to completing and submitting data for the WHO global survey
constraints: Designed for simulation training purposes to achieve standardization and interactive learning
target_learning_goals: correct standardized completion of the HHSAF
examples: Case Scenario 1 (Bellevue University Medical Centre) scored 377.5/500; Case Scenario 2 (St. Mary's Teaching Hospital, Uganda) scored 80/500; Case Scenario 3 (Ulwazi National Referral Hospital) scored 120/500
key_sources: Tartari E, Fankhauser C, Peters A, Sithole BL, Timurkaynak F, Masson-Roy S, Allegranzi B, Pires D, Pittet D. (2019). Scenario-based simulation training for the WHO hand hygiene self-assessment framework. Antimicrobial Resistance and Infection Control. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13756-019-0511-9

article_title: The communication skills course for second year medical students at Hannover Medical School: An evaluation study based on students' self-assessments.
citation: von Lengerke Thomas, Kursch Angelika, Lange Karin, APG-Lehrteam MHH. (2011). The communication skills course for second year medical students at Hannover Medical School: An evaluation study based on students' self-assessments. GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung 28(4), Doc54. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3244738/
title: 28-hour second-year doctor-patient communication course (HannibaL, MHH) with simulated patients, role play and OSCE-aligned observation sheets
description: A 28-hour, seven-session doctor-patient communication course in the second year of the HannibaL curriculum at Hannover Medical School, taught in groups of ten students. Its learning objectives are 'basic skills in taking patient histories, disclosing diagnoses (breaking bad news), and the use of shared decision-making (SDM) in these contexts', assessed at two of six OSCE stations; simulated patients join three of the seven sessions.
requirements: Small groups of ten students to allow repeated role play within the group and with the simulated patients
A pool of about 80 trained simulated patients and observation sheets combining the Calgary-Cambridge Guides criteria with those of Füeßl and Middeke
constraints: The article notes that implementing practice-oriented teaching in small groups using SP 'requires significant personnel, organisational and financial resources'
examples: In the 2009/10 academic year, 285 students took the course; two SP per group of ten enabled up to eight role plays per course group in the fourth session, and predefined cases covered diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, coronary heart disease and other OSCE-relevant diseases.
key_sources: von Lengerke Thomas, Kursch Angelika, Lange Karin, APG-Lehrteam MHH. (2011). The communication skills course for second year medical students at Hannover Medical School: An evaluation study based on students' self-assessments. GMS Zeitschrift für Medizinische Ausbildung 28(4), Doc54. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3244738/
